You are a code snippet reviewer. Your task is to review the code_snippets array and determine which snippets contain ACTUAL executable code vs documentation/text.

KEEP snippets that contain:
- Actual code blocks (JSON, Python, JavaScript, Bash, YAML, SQL, etc.)
- Complete functions, classes, or code structures
- Configuration files (JSON, YAML, XML)
- API requests/responses with actual data
- Command-line examples that are executable

REMOVE snippets that are:
- Just field descriptions (e.g., "* `field`: Description text")
- Bullet point lists without executable code
- Plain text documentation
- Log messages or error messages (unless showing actual code context)
- Single-line field/property descriptions
- Markdown formatting without code substance

EXAMPLES:

KEEP:
```json
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0",
  "id": 1,
  "method": "completion/complete"
}
```

KEEP:
```python
def calculate_total(items):
    return sum(item.price for item in items)
```

"* `role`: Either "user" or "assistant" to indicate the speaker"

REMOVE:
"* `completion`: Object containing:\n  + `values`: Array of suggestions"

"Field description: The name of the user"

- removed_snippets: Array of snippets that were removed
- removal_reasoning: Brief explanation of why snippets were removed

{"summary_title": "dbt grants and permissions (overview)", "summary_content": "dbt Core v1.2 introduced a structured grants config that lets dbt manage object-level permissions for models and other resources. Grants are declared as a dictionary (for example, {'select': ['role']}) and dbt chooses the most efficient path to apply those grants rather than requiring manual SQL for every permission. If a resource has no grants config or it is set to {{ }}, dbt will not manage grants for that object.

When grants change, dbt computes the diff between the desired and current permissions and can emit REVOKE statements as part of the update process; these REVOKE statements are visible at debug log level. dbt knows whether existing grants should be "carried over" for incremental model runs based on the model's materialization and the target database. Grants are exposed in dbt metadata and the project graph, enabling macros to iterate graph.nodes to infer or aggregate schema-level grant information.

Schemas are not modeled as first-class configurable objects in dbt, so schema-level USAGE grants still need to be applied via hooks or post-hooks. Database-specific advanced permission features (for example, Snowflake row access policies or column masking policies) also require post-hooks to apply. The ability to manage grants is a global capability: users operating with the transformer role can change grants on any object as if they were the owner. Use post-hooks to grant permissions to other transformers and BI users so model changes remain accessible to collaborators.", "key_concepts": ["dbt v1.2 adds a structured grants config for resources.", "Configure grants as a dictionary (e.g., {'select': ['role']}); omit or set to {{}} to prevent dbt from managing grants.", "dbt computes diffs and can issue REVOKE statements when permissions change (visible at debug level).", "Grant carry-over behavior for incremental models depends on materialization and the target database.", "Schemas are not first-class objects in dbt; schema USAGE and advanced DB-specific policies require hooks/post-hooks."], "technical_details": "- grants syntax: a structured dictionary mapping privileges to principal lists — example: {'select': ['role']}
- If grants is missing or set to {{ }}, dbt will not manage grants for that object
- dbt selects the most efficient SQL path to apply grants rather than requiring explicit SQL
- On grant changes, dbt computes diffs and may issue REVOKE statements; REVOKE activity appears in debug logs
- dbt determines whether to carry over existing grants for incremental models based on materialization type and the target database
- grants are available via dbt metadata/graph so macros can inspect graph.nodes to infer schema-level grant distributions
- Schema-level USAGE grants are not managed via the grants config and must be applied with hooks/post-hooks
- Database-specific features (e.g., Snowflake row access policies and column masking) require post-hooks to attach policies to objects
- Grant-management is global: a user with the transformer role can alter grants on any object as if they own it
- Use post-hooks to grant permissions to other transformers and BI users so collaborators retain access after model changes", "code_snippets": ["{'select': ['role']}", "{{}}"], "learning_objectives": ["Configure grants in dbt using a structured dictionary (e.g., {'select': ['role']}).", "Apply post-hooks to grant schema USAGE and to attach database-specific policies (row access, masking).", "Analyze debug logs to verify grant diffs and any REVOKE statements issued during grant updates.", "Integrate grants into macros via dbt metadata/graph to infer or aggregate schema-level permissions."]}

{"summary_title": "dbt generate_model_yaml: usage, workflow, and validation", "summary_content": "The generate_model_yaml dbt macro creates schema YAML for one or more models. It requires the model_names parameter and optionally includes upstream column descriptions when upstream_descriptions=True (default is False). A single call can combine multiple model definitions into one .yml output.

Model names can be provided programmatically (for example, by piping the output of dbt ls) or listed explicitly. Documentation text can be stored in docs blocks using the {{% docs <name> %}} ... {{% enddocs %}} syntax and then referenced in generated schema YAML with the doc('<name>') function. After generating or editing YAML, run dbt docs generate to validate YAML syntax before serving docs.

Prefer adding new docs or docs blocks manually when adding new models or adding columns to existing models rather than fully automated replacements. Regex and command behavior may vary across platforms; verify outputs in your environment (examples were tested on Mac/VS Code).", "key_concepts": ["model_names is required when invoking generate_model_yaml.", "upstream_descriptions is optional and defaults to False; set it to True to include identical column names' descriptions from upstream models.", "A single generate_model_yaml call can output a combined .yml for multiple models.", "Create docs blocks with {{% docs <name> %}}...{{% enddocs %}} and reference them in schema YAML via {{ doc('<name>') }}.", "Run dbt docs generate to validate YAML and catch syntax errors before serving documentation."], "technical_details": "- model_names (required): supply one or more model names (string or list of strings).
- upstream_descriptions (optional, default=False): Boolean to include identical column names' descriptions from upstream models.
- To combine multiple models into one YAML, pass multiple names in model_names in a single call.
- Use dbt ls -m <path> --output name to list model names programmatically for piping into generate_model_yaml.
- After generating or editing YAML, run dbt docs generate to validate YAML syntax prior to running dbt docs serve.
- Add docs text using the docs block syntax: {{% docs <name> %}}...{{% enddocs %}} and reference it in schema YAML via {{ doc('<name>') }}.
- Prefer manual addition of docs/doc-blocks when adding models or columns to existing folders to avoid overwriting or incorrect replacements.
- Be aware that regex and shell behavior can vary by platform (the provided approach was tested on Mac/VS Code).", "code_snippets": ["$ dbt run-operation generate_model_yaml --args '{{"model_names": [ "activity_based_interest_activated", "activity_based_interest_deactivated", "activity_based_interest_updated", ...] }}'", "$ dbt ls -m models/core/activity_based_interest --output name | xargs -I{{}} echo -n ' "{{}}",'", "$ cat .../_activity_based_interest_docs.md  {{% docs activity_based_interest__id %}} ... {{% enddocs %}
$ cat .../_activity_based_interest_docs.yml  ... description: "{{{{ doc('activity_based_interest__id') }}}}""], "learning_objectives": ["Identify the required and optional parameters for generate_model_yaml (model_names, upstream_descriptions).", "Apply dbt ls with --output name to programmatically gather model names for generate_model_yaml inputs.", "Configure generate_model_yaml to emit a single combined .yml when passing multiple model_names.", "Analyze generated YAML with dbt docs generate to detect and resolve syntax errors before serving documentation."]}

{"summary_title": "Extract unique column names with grep, cut and sort", "summary_content": "Use a short shell pipeline to extract the values of YAML "- name:" entries and produce a deduplicated list. The pipeline locates lines that contain the indented "- name:" property, strips the leading indentation and marker, and then sorts and uniquifies the resulting names.

Each stage performs a single transformation: grep filters for the property lines, cut removes the fixed-width prefix to leave only the name value, and sort -u sorts alphabetically while removing duplicates. Run the pipeline against each file (or iterate files) to collect unique column names across a folder.", "key_concepts": ["grep '      \- name:' matches lines that contain six spaces followed by '- name:'.", "cut -c 15- removes the first 14 characters of each matched line, leaving the name value.", "sort -u sorts the output and removes duplicate entries, producing a unique list.", "The pipeline yields a deduplicated, sorted list of the YAML name values."], "technical_details": "• Command pipeline: grep '      \- name:' <file> | cut -c 15- | sort -u
• grep pattern and quoting: the pattern includes leading spaces and an escaped hyphen; wrap the pattern in single quotes to prevent shell interpretation.
• cut -c 15-: select characters from position 15 through end (removes the first 14 characters which include indentation and the "- name:" marker plus following space).
• sort -u: sort lines and remove duplicates to produce a unique list.
• File target: replace <file> with the YAML file path; run the pipeline per file or across multiple files to aggregate results.
• Leading '$' in examples denotes the shell prompt and is not part of the command to type.", "code_snippets": ["$ grep '      \\- name:' models/core/activity_based_interest/_activity_based_interest_docs.yml | cut -c 15- | sort -u"], "learning_objectives": ["Apply the grep | cut | sort pipeline to extract unique column names from YAML files.", "Extract the name values by trimming the first 14 characters with cut -c 15-.", "Produce a deduplicated, sorted list of name entries using sort -u."]}
